answers.question: When our company's data protection officer does their job, do they have to pay more attention to the riskier ways we handle people's information?
answers.answer: Yes. When performing their tasks, your data protection officer must give due regard to the risks associated with processing personal data, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of that processing. [c1] This means giving attention to risk in how they carry out their duties, which include advising on data protection obligations and monitoring compliance. [c1][c2]
answers.reason: The answer accurately paraphrases Art. 39(2) [c1] on due regard to risk and correctly cites Art. 39(1) [c2] for the DPO's advising and monitoring tasks.

answers.question: If a company has posted my personal information online and has to delete it because I asked, does it also have to tell other websites that copied or linked to it that I want it removed?
answers.answer:
Yes. If the company made your personal data public and is obliged to erase it under Article 17(1), it must take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform other controllers processing that data that you have requested deletion of links to it, or copies or replications of it. It must take account of available technology and implementation costs; the obligation is to take reasonable steps, not to guarantee removal everywhere. [c1]

It must also communicate erasure carried out under Article 17(1) to each recipient to whom it disclosed the data, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort. If you ask, it must tell you about those recipients. [c3]
answers.reason: The first paragraph restates Art. 17(2) (reasonable steps, technical measures, available technology and cost) and the second restates Art. 19 (notify recipients unless impossible or disproportionate effort, and tell the data subject about them on request), with each citation matching its claim.

answers.question: Where can I find an official list of countries that have been approved, or no longer approved, as having good enough data protection for sending personal information abroad?
answers.answer: The European Commission publishes the official list in the **Official Journal of the European Union** and on **its website**, covering third countries, territories, specified sectors within third countries, and international organisations that it has decided do—or no longer—ensure an adequate level of data protection. [c1]
answers.reason: The answer restates Art. 45(8) (c1): the Commission publishes the list in the Official Journal and on its website, covering countries, territories, sectors and international organisations with an adequate level of protection ensured or no longer ensured.

answers.question: Can the European body that coordinates data protection regulators be told what to do by outside parties like governments or companies when it carries out its work?
answers.answer: No. The Board must act independently when performing its tasks or exercising its powers, and must neither seek nor take instructions from anybody—including governments or companies—subject to the provision preserving certain Commission requests referred to in Article 70(1)(b) and Article 70(2). [c1][c2]
answers.reason: Art. 69(1) and 69(2) support the claims that the Board acts independently and neither seeks nor takes instructions from anybody, with the Commission-request carve-out; 'including governments or companies' is a fair reading of 'anybody'.

answers.question: Does a small partnership or club that regularly earns money count as a business under the data protection rules, even if it isn't a formal company?
answers.answer:
Yes—if it regularly engages in economic activity, a partnership or club can count as an “enterprise” under the GDPR even if it is not a formal company: the definition applies regardless of legal form and includes partnerships or associations regularly engaged in economic activity. [c1]

Whether the GDPR applies to its data processing depends on whether it processes personal data wholly or partly by automated means, or processes it manually as part of—or intended for—a filing system. [c3]
answers.reason: The first claim matches Art. 4(18) in [c1], which covers partnerships or associations regularly engaged in an economic activity regardless of legal form, and the second claim restates the scope of Art. 2(1) in [c3].

answers.question: If I agree to let a company use my personal details, can I change my mind later, and should stopping be just as simple as signing up?
answers.answer:
Yes. If you give consent to a company’s use of your personal data, you have the right to withdraw it at any time, and withdrawing must be as easy as giving consent. [c1]

The company must inform you of this before you consent; withdrawing does not affect the lawfulness of processing based on your consent before you withdrew it. [c1]
answers.reason: Every claim (right to withdraw at any time, withdrawal as easy as giving consent, prior information, no retroactive effect on earlier processing) is stated in Art. 7(3) [c1], which is the only source cited.

answers.question: Does the data protection regulator in my country have to keep its own log of companies that broke the privacy rules and what penalties or corrective steps it imposed on them?
answers.answer:
Yes. Each supervisory authority must keep internal records of infringements of the GDPR and of measures taken under Article 58(2) within its territory. [c1]

This is an internal record-keeping duty; the authority must also publish an annual activity report, but including a list of types of infringements notified and types of measures taken is optional. [c1][c2] The provided sources do not specify which penalties or corrective steps fall under Article 58(2). [c1][c2]
answers.reason: Art. 57(1)(u) supports the internal-records duty, Art. 59 supports the annual report being mandatory with the list of infringement and measure types optional ('may include'), and the sources do indeed not list the Art. 58(2) measures.

answers.question: Can an organization use my sensitive details, like health or religion information, without my consent if it's done for an important public benefit that a law allows and protects me?
answers.answer:
Yes—processing special categories of personal data without consent can be permitted where it is necessary for reasons of **substantial public interest** and is based on Union or Member State law that is proportionate to the aim pursued, respects the essence of your right to data protection, and provides suitable, specific measures to safeguard your fundamental rights and interests. [c1]

For public health, processing can also be permitted where it is necessary for public-interest reasons and based on Union or Member State law providing suitable, specific safeguards for your rights and freedoms, particularly professional secrecy; Recital 54 expressly recognises that such processing may occur without consent. [c2][c6]
answers.reason: The first paragraph accurately restates Art. 9(2)(g) [c1]; the second paragraph accurately restates Art. 9(2)(i) [c2] and Recital 54's statement that such public-health processing may occur without consent [c6].

answers.question: What does a company have to prove before it is allowed to hand out data protection certificates or seals to other businesses?
answers.answer:
To issue data protection certificates or seals as a certification body, a company must have appropriate data protection expertise and be accredited by the competent supervisory authority, the national accreditation body, or both. [c2]

To obtain accreditation, it must: [c1]
- Demonstrate its independence and expertise in the certification’s subject matter to the competent supervisory authority’s satisfaction. [c1]
- Commit to respecting certification criteria approved by the competent supervisory authority or the Board. [c1]
- Establish procedures for issuing, periodically reviewing and withdrawing data protection certifications, seals and marks. [c1]
- Establish procedures and structures for handling complaints about certification infringements or how a controller or processor implements certification, and make those procedures and structures transparent to data subjects and the public. [c1]
- Demonstrate, to the competent supervisory authority’s satisfaction, that its tasks and duties do not create a conflict of interests. [c1]

Accreditation must be based on criteria approved by the competent supervisory authority or the Board; accreditation through the national accreditation body must also comply with EN-ISO/IEC 17065/2012 and the supervisory authority’s additional requirements. [c2][c3]

Before issuing or renewing certification, the body must inform the supervisory authority so that it can exercise its powers where necessary; certification must be based on approved criteria. [c2][c4]
answers.reason: Each claim matches the sources: Art. 43(1) for expertise, accreditation routes and informing the authority, Art. 43(2) for the five accreditation requirements, Art. 43(3) for approved criteria, and Art. 42(5) for certification on approved criteria.

answers.question: If a data protection authority in another country asks for help with my case, can they use the information they receive for anything other than the reason they asked for it?
answers.answer:
Under Article 61’s mutual-assistance rules, no: information exchanged between supervisory authorities may be used only for the purpose for which it was requested, and the request must state its purpose and reasons. [c1]

For cooperation with authorities in countries outside the EU, the sources require appropriate safeguards but do not specify whether received information may be used for other purposes. [c3][c6]
answers.reason: Art. 61(3) [c1] directly supports the purpose-limitation answer, and the sources do say that third-country cooperation is subject to appropriate safeguards [c3] and say nothing about other uses of received information [c3][c6].

answers.question: What does it mean when the data protection rules talk about an online service, and where can I find the official description of that term?
answers.answer:
The formal term used in these sources is “information society service.” Article 4(25) defines it by reference to point (b) of Article 1(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/1535—that is where to find the official description. [c1]

The supplied sources do not reproduce that description, so they do not explain which online services fall within the definition. [c1]
answers.reason: Art. 4(25) in [c1] defines 'information society service' by reference to point (b) of Article 1(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/1535, and the sources do not reproduce that definition, so both claims are supported.

answers.question: Does the national data protection authority in my country give advice to the government and lawmakers when they are drafting new rules that affect people's privacy?
answers.answer:
Yes. Each supervisory authority must, within its territory and in accordance with Member State law, advise the national parliament, government, and other institutions and bodies on legislative and administrative measures relating to people’s rights and freedoms in connection with personal data processing. [c1]

Member States must consult the authority while preparing proposed legislation for a national parliament, or regulatory measures based on such legislation, that relate to processing. [c2] The authority can also issue opinions, on its own initiative or on request, to the national parliament and government on any issue related to personal data protection. [c4]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: Art. 57(1)(c) covers the advisory task [c1], Art. 36(4) covers mandatory consultation during drafting [c2], and Art. 58(3)(b) covers opinions on the authority's own initiative or on request [c4].

answers.question: If I hire an outside company to handle my customers' data, what must our agreement say about the company only acting on my written instructions, including sending data abroad?
answers.answer:
Your agreement must say that the company, as processor, will process personal data only on your documented instructions as controller, including instructions about transferring data to a third country or an international organisation. [c1]

It must allow an exception where processing is required by Union or Member State law to which the company is subject; in that case, the company must inform you of the legal requirement before processing, unless that law prohibits informing you on important grounds of public interest. [c1]

The agreement must be in writing, which can include electronic form. [c4] It must also require the company to inform you immediately if, in its opinion, an instruction infringes the GDPR or other Union or Member State data protection provisions. [c6]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: c1 for documented instructions, transfers and the legal-requirement exception, c4 for the writing requirement, and c6 for the duty to flag infringing instructions.

answers.question: If I send a saliva sample to a DNA testing company, does the information about my body and health that they get from it count as a special kind of personal data?
answers.answer:
Yes—if the information relates to you as an identified or identifiable person, DNA analysis of your saliva that reveals your inherited or acquired genetic characteristics and gives unique information about your physiology or health counts as **genetic data**. [c1][c2][c6]

Information revealing your physical or mental health status also counts as **data concerning health**, including information derived from testing bodily substances or biological samples. [c3][c4]

Both genetic data and data concerning health are **special categories of personal data** under Article 9. [c5]
answers.reason: The answer follows the definitions in Art. 4(13), Recital 34, Art. 4(15) and Recital 35, and Art. 9(1) lists genetic data and health data among the specially treated categories. The label 'special categories' is not in the quoted text, but it is a fair reading of that list.

answers.question: Can my employer handle sensitive details about me, like health information, if it's needed to meet job-related legal duties such as sick pay or social security rules?
answers.answer:
Yes, if the processing is necessary to meet obligations or exercise specific rights in employment, social security or social protection law, and is authorised by Union or Member State law or a collective agreement under Member State law that provides appropriate safeguards for your fundamental rights and interests. [c1]

Your employer must also have a lawful basis for the processing; this can be that it is necessary to comply with a legal obligation to which the employer is subject. [c3]

Member States may set more specific rules for processing employees’ personal data, and those rules must include suitable, specific safeguards for employees’ dignity, legitimate interests and fundamental rights. [c2][c5]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: Art. 9(2)(b) for the employment-law exception, Art. 6(1)(c) for the legal-obligation basis, and Art. 88(1) and 88(2) for the Member State rules and safeguards.

answers.question: If a court in a non-EU country orders my company to hand over customer data, do we have to comply right away?
answers.answer:
Not automatically: a non-EU court order requiring a controller or processor to disclose personal data may be recognised or enforced only if it is based on an international agreement in force between that country and the EU or a Member State, such as a mutual legal assistance treaty; this does not rule out other grounds for transfer under Chapter V. [c1]

Any transfer must meet the GDPR’s conditions for transfers to third countries; the court order alone does not replace those conditions. [c2][c3] In the absence of an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, possible grounds include a transfer necessary for important reasons of public interest or for establishing, exercising or defending legal claims. [c4][c5] For the public-interest ground, the disclosure must be necessary for an important public interest recognised in EU or Member State law to which your company is subject. [c2]

The sources do not establish whether your particular order is enforceable or what deadline applies, so they do not establish that you must comply right away. [c1][c2]
answers.reason: The answer says the public-interest ground 'must' rest on an interest recognised in EU or Member State law and cites [c2], but c2 only says a transfer 'may' be allowed in that case, as an example, and does not state a requirement.

answers.question: If my company shares personal data between its branches in different countries under internal company rules, how must those rules explain to people how they will be told about their rights and protections, beyond the usual privacy notices?
answers.answer:
If your company uses binding corporate rules, those rules must specify how information about them will be provided to the people whose data is processed, in addition to the information required by Articles 13 and 14. [c1]

That must cover, in particular, people’s rights and how to exercise them—including the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, in accordance with Article 22; complaints to the competent supervisory authority and proceedings before competent Member State courts; and redress and, where appropriate, compensation for breaches of the rules. [c1][c2]

It must also cover the acceptance of liability by a controller or processor established in a Member State for breaches by a covered member outside the EU, including the condition that it is exempt, wholly or partly, only if it proves that member was not responsible for the event causing the damage. [c1][c6]
answers.reason: The answer accurately reflects Art. 47(2)(g), which requires information on points (d), (e) and (f) to be provided in addition to Arts. 13 and 14, and its details on data subject rights (c2) and liability (c6) match those sources.

answers.question: If a company wants to use the information it collected from me for a new reason I never agreed to, what should it think about to decide whether the new use is still acceptable?
answers.answer:
If the new use is not based on your consent or on a Union or Member State law that meets the necessary-and-proportionate conditions in Article 6(4), the company must assess whether it is compatible with the original purpose, taking into account at least these factors: [c1]

- How closely the original purpose and the proposed new purpose are linked. [c1]
- The circumstances in which your information was collected, including your relationship with the company and what further use you could reasonably expect. [c1][c2]
- The nature of the information, particularly whether it includes special categories of personal data or information about criminal convictions and offences. [c1]
- The possible consequences of the new use for you. [c1]
- Whether appropriate safeguards exist, which may include encryption or pseudonymisation. [c1]

If the new use is compatible, no separate legal basis from the one that allowed the original collection is required; the GDPR’s principles must still be followed. [c2] The company must also tell you about the new purpose before starting that further processing and provide any relevant further information required under Article 13(3). [c5]
answers.reason: Each point matches its source: the five Art. 6(4) factors come from c1, the reasonable-expectations wording from c2, the no-separate-legal-basis and principles points from c2, and the prior-notice duty from Art. 13(3) in c5.

answers.question: If a company I hired to handle data starts deciding for itself why and how to use that data, does it become responsible like the owner of the data?
answers.answer:
Yes—if the company is acting as your processor and infringes the GDPR by deciding the purposes and means of processing (why and how personal data is used), it is treated as a controller for that processing. [c1] “Controller” describes who determines those purposes and means, rather than who owns the data. [c2]

That can include liability for damage: where multiple controllers or processors are involved in the same processing and are responsible for damage under Article 82(2) and (3), each is liable for the entire damage to ensure effective compensation. [c6] The supplied sources do not set out the conditions in those two paragraphs. [c6]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its source: c1 says a processor that determines purposes and means is treated as a controller, c2 defines a controller by who determines purposes and means, and c6 provides joint liability for the entire damage and refers to paragraphs 2 and 3 without setting out their conditions.

answers.question: Can our church or club keep records about our members' beliefs without asking each person's permission, as long as we don't share the information with anyone outside the group?
answers.answer:
Yes, but keeping the information inside the group is not enough on its own: your church or club must be a not-for-profit body with a political, philosophical, religious or trade union aim, and the processing must be part of its legitimate activities with appropriate safeguards. [c2]

Under this exception, the information must relate solely to members, former members, or people who have regular contact with the body in connection with its purposes; it must not be disclosed outside the body without those people’s consent. [c2] If all these conditions are met, the exception allows processing of members’ beliefs without obtaining each person’s explicit consent. [c1][c2]
answers.reason: The answer accurately restates the Art. 9(2)(d) conditions (not-for-profit body with a relevant aim, legitimate activities with safeguards, processing limited to members, former members and regular contacts, no disclosure outside without consent), and c1 supports the general prohibition that this exception lifts.

answers.question: Can the data protection authority in my country take a company that broke privacy rules to court?
answers.answer:
Yes—each Member State must give its data protection authority the legal power to bring GDPR infringements to the attention of judicial authorities and, where appropriate, to start or otherwise take part in legal proceedings to enforce the GDPR. [c1]

An authority is competent to handle a complaint or possible infringement if it relates only to an establishment in its Member State or substantially affects data subjects only in that Member State. [c2] The sources do not establish whether your country’s authority can act against the particular company you have in mind. [c1][c2]
answers.reason: The first paragraph restates Art. 58(5) [c1], the competence claim accurately paraphrases Art. 56(2) [c2], and the closing caveat about the sources' limits is a fair statement that does not add unsupported facts.

answers.question: If our company's internal data-sharing rules for international transfers get updated, how do we have to keep track of the changes and let the data protection regulator know?
answers.answer:
If your company’s rules are binding corporate rules, they must specify mechanisms for recording and reporting changes to the rules, including reporting those changes to the supervisory authority (the data protection regulator). [c1]

The supplied sources do not specify a reporting deadline, a required format, or detailed notification steps; Article 47(3) says the Commission may specify formats and procedures for exchanging information about binding corporate rules. [c1][c4]
answers.reason: Art. 47(2)(k) [c1] supports the requirement to record changes and report them to the supervisory authority, and Art. 47(3) [c4] supports the Commission's power to specify formats and procedures; the statement that no deadline or format is given is accurate for the sources.

answers.question: What counts as a global organization, like a group created by an agreement between several countries, when it comes to handling my personal data?
answers.answer:
The GDPR calls this an “international organisation”: an organisation and its subordinate bodies governed by public international law, or any other body set up by, or on the basis of, an agreement between two or more countries. [c1]

Personal data may be transferred to such an organisation where the European Commission has decided that it ensures an adequate level of protection; that transfer does not require specific authorisation. [c2]
answers.reason: The definition in the first paragraph matches Art. 4(26) [c1], and the adequacy-decision transfer without specific authorisation matches Art. 45(1) [c2].

answers.question: If a data protection authority leading a cross-border case agrees with another country's regulator who objected to its proposed decision, what happens next and how quickly do they have to respond?
answers.answer:
If the lead authority intends to follow the relevant and reasoned objection, it must send a revised draft decision to the other supervisory authorities concerned for their opinion. [c1]

Those authorities have two weeks to raise a relevant and reasoned objection to the revised draft. [c1][c4] If none objects within that period, the lead authority and the other authorities concerned are deemed to agree with the draft and are bound by it. [c2]

The lead authority must then adopt the decision and notify the controller’s or processor’s main or single establishment, and inform the other authorities concerned and the Board; the authority that received the complaint must inform the complainant. [c3]
answers.reason: Each claim matches the sources: a revised draft goes to the other authorities with a two-week period (c1), objections follow the Art. 60(4) procedure (c4), silence means deemed agreement and being bound (c2), and the lead authority then adopts and notifies the decision (c3).

answers.question: Who decides what the little standardised pictures that explain how my data is used should show, and how companies should provide them?
answers.answer: The European Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts determining what information the standardised icons should show and the procedures for providing them. [c1] The Board’s role is to give the Commission an opinion on those icons. [c2]
answers.reason: Art. 12(8) [c1] empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts on the icons' information and the procedures for providing them, and Art. 70(1)(r) [c2] has the Board give the Commission an opinion on the icons, so both claims are supported.

answers.question: If I hire an outside company to handle my customers' data, does our contract have to say they'll help me meet my security, breach-reporting, and risk-assessment duties?
answers.answer:
Yes—if you are the controller and the outside company is your processor, your contract (or another binding legal act under Union or Member State law) must require it to help you comply with the obligations under Articles 32–36, taking into account the nature of the processing and the information available to it. [c1] It must also require the processor to take all measures required by Article 32. [c2]

Those duties include risk-appropriate security measures; notifying the competent supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to risk individuals’ rights and freedoms; and notifying affected individuals without undue delay when a breach is likely to pose a high risk. [c3][c4][c6] They also include, where necessary, reviewing whether processing follows the data protection impact assessment, at least when the risk represented by the processing changes. [c5]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: c1 for assistance with Arts. 32–36, c2 for Art. 32 measures, c3, c4 and c6 for security and the two breach notifications, and c5 for the DPIA review.

answers.question: If national data protection regulators disagree about my company's case and it goes to the EU-level group of regulators for review, can any of them issue their own ruling while that review is still going on?
answers.answer:
No. The supervisory authorities concerned must not issue a decision on the subject matter referred to the Board during the review periods specified in Article 65(2) and (3). [c1]

The Board normally has one month from referral to adopt its binding decision; this may be extended by a further month because of the case’s complexity. [c3]

After the Board notifies its decision, the lead supervisory authority—or, where applicable, the authority with which the complaint was lodged—must adopt its final decision based on the Board’s decision, without undue delay and within one month at the latest. [c5]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: c1 bars decisions by supervisory authorities concerned during the periods in Art. 65(2)-(3), c3 gives the one-month period with a one-month extension, and c5 sets the final-decision deadline.

answers.question: If the European data protection authorities can't reach a decision on a cross-border dispute in time, how is the final decision made, and who breaks the tie if the vote is evenly split?
answers.answer:
If the Board cannot reach a decision within the initial one-month period, which may be extended by a further month because of the matter’s complexity, it must decide within two weeks after the second month expires, by a simple majority of its members. If the vote is evenly split, the Board’s Chair breaks the tie. [c2][c1]

The lead supervisory authority—or, where applicable, the authority with which the complaint was lodged—then adopts its final decision based on the Board’s binding decision, without undue delay and no later than one month after the Board notifies its decision. [c2][c3]
answers.reason: The answer matches Art. 65(2), 65(3) and 65(6): a one-month period extendable by one month, then two more weeks with a simple majority, the Chair's vote deciding a split, and the final national decision within one month of notification. The [c2] tag on the second paragraph is only loosely supportive, since c2 just describes the decision as binding, but it is not wrong.

answers.question: What basic rules does a company have to follow when it collects, uses, stores, and protects my personal information?
answers.answer:
A company must follow these basic rules when handling your personal information:

- **Be lawful, fair and transparent.** It must have a lawful basis for processing, such as your consent for specific purposes, necessity for a contract with you, or compliance with a legal obligation; consent is not the only possible basis. [c1][c2]
- **Use it for clear purposes.** It must collect information for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not use it further in ways incompatible with those purposes. [c1]
- **Collect and use only what is needed.** Your information must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing. [c1]
- **Keep it accurate.** It must take every reasonable step to correct or erase inaccurate information without delay, taking account of the purposes for which it is used. [c1]
- **Limit how long it keeps it.** Information that identifies you must not be kept longer than necessary; longer storage is permitted solely for public-interest archiving, scientific or historical research, or statistical purposes, subject to the specified safeguards and conditions. [c1]
- **Protect it.** It must use appropriate technical or organisational measures to protect against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage. [c1]

When the company collects information directly from you, it must tell you at that time who it is and how to contact it, its purposes and legal basis, and any recipients or categories of recipients. [c4] Where applicable, it must also provide its representative’s and data protection officer’s contact details, explain the legitimate interests relied on, and provide the specified information about intended international transfers and safeguards. [c4] Information about processing should be easy to access and understand, using clear, plain language. [c3]

The company must build appropriate safeguards into how it designs and carries out processing, taking account of available technology, implementation costs, the processing’s nature, scope, context and purposes, and risks to people’s rights and freedoms. [c5] By default, it must limit the amount collected, use, storage period and accessibility to what is necessary for each specific purpose, and must not make your information accessible to an indefinite number of people without your intervention. [c6]
answers.reason: Each point matches the cited text: c1 for the Art. 5 principles, c2 for the lawful bases, c3 for plain-language transparency, c4 for the Art. 13 information duties, and c5 and c6 for the Art. 25 design and default duties.

answers.question: If a privacy regulator in one EU country thinks people's data needs protecting right away, can it skip the usual slow process of working with the main regulator on a case?
answers.answer:
Yes—in exceptional circumstances, if a supervisory authority concerned considers urgent action necessary to protect people’s rights and freedoms, it may bypass the usual cooperation or consistency procedure and immediately adopt provisional measures that have legal effect only in its own territory. Those measures must have a specified validity period of no more than three months. [c1]

It must, without delay, communicate the measures and its reasons to the other supervisory authorities concerned, the Board and the Commission. [c1]
answers.reason: Every claim in the answer (exceptional circumstances, derogation from the cooperation and consistency procedures, provisional measures with legal effect on its own territory, a validity period of at most three months, and communication without delay to the other supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission) is directly supported by Art. 66(1) [c1], which is the source cited.

answers.question: When can a data protection regulator in one EU country turn down another country's regulator who asks for help with a privacy case?
answers.answer:
A requested data protection regulator may refuse another regulator’s request for assistance only if:
- It is not competent to deal with the subject matter or carry out the requested measures; or
- Complying would breach the GDPR, EU law, or Member State law that applies to the requested regulator. [c1]

The regulator must give reasons for any refusal. [c2] It must take all appropriate measures needed to reply without undue delay, and no later than one month after receiving the request. [c3]
answers.reason: The two refusal grounds (c1), the duty to give reasons (c2), and the one-month, no-undue-delay reply duty (c3) are all accurately paraphrased and correctly cited.

answers.question: If the EU approved a country's data protection standards under the old privacy law from before 2018, is that approval still valid today?
answers.answer:
Yes—if you mean a Commission decision adopted under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC, it remains in force unless it has been amended, replaced or repealed by a Commission decision under Article 45(3) or (5). [c1]

The old Directive’s repeal on 25 May 2018 did not itself end those approvals. [c1][c6] The sources do not establish whether any particular country’s approval remains in force today. [c1]
answers.reason: Art. 45(9) (c1) supports the continued validity of Art. 25(6) decisions until amended, replaced or repealed under Art. 45(3) or (5), c6 supports the 25 May 2018 repeal date, and the caveat about specific countries is a fair limit on what the sources show.

answers.question: What are the internal company data protection policies that let a business group send personal information to its branches or partner companies in countries outside the EU?
answers.answer:
They are called **binding corporate rules (BCRs)**: personal data protection policies followed by a controller or processor established in an EU Member State for transfers to controllers or processors in third countries within the same group of undertakings, or group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity—not partner companies generally. [c1]

The competent supervisory authority must approve them, provided they are legally binding and enforced by every group member concerned, including employees; expressly give individuals enforceable rights over the processing of their personal data; and meet Article 47(2)’s requirements. [c2]
answers.reason: The answer closely paraphrases Art. 4(20) for the definition and Art. 47(1) for the approval conditions, and the remark that partner companies generally are not covered is a fair reading of the 'group of undertakings or joint economic activity' wording.

answers.question: If I hire an outside company to handle my customers' information, does our contract have to say they'll help me answer people who ask to see or fix their data?
answers.answer:
Yes—if the outside company processes your customers’ personal data on your behalf, the contract or other binding legal act must require it to help you respond to requests to exercise data subjects’ rights, using appropriate technical and organisational measures, insofar as possible and taking account of the nature of the processing. [c1]

That contract or legal act must be in writing, which can include electronic form. [c3]
answers.reason: Both claims (processor assistance with data subject requests per Art. 28(3)(e), and writing/electronic form per Art. 28(9)) are directly supported by the cited sources [c1] and [c3].

answers.question: If my company is based outside Europe, who is the person or business we have to appoint in writing to act for us on our data protection duties inside the EU?
answers.answer:
That is an **EU representative**: a person or legal entity established in the EU, appointed in writing to represent your company regarding its GDPR obligations. [c1]

You must appoint one if your company is not established in the EU and processes personal data of people in the EU in connection with offering them goods or services (whether paid or free), or monitoring their behaviour within the EU, unless an exemption applies. [c2][c3][c5]

The exemptions cover a public authority or body, or processing that is occasional, does not include large-scale processing of special-category data or data relating to criminal convictions and offences, and is unlikely to risk people’s rights and freedoms, taking account of its nature, context, scope and purposes. [c5]

The representative must be established in an EU Member State where the people whose data you process in connection with those goods or services, or whose behaviour you monitor, are located. [c6]
answers.reason: Every claim (definition, duty to designate in writing, scope under Art. 3(2), exemptions, and establishment location) matches the cited sources.

answers.question: If a company operates in several EU countries and is investigated over a data problem, do the different national privacy regulators have to work together and share what they know?
answers.answer:
Yes. Each supervisory authority must cooperate with other supervisory authorities, including sharing information and providing mutual assistance, to ensure consistent application and enforcement of the GDPR. [c5]

Where a lead supervisory authority is involved, it must cooperate with the other authorities concerned in an effort to reach consensus, and they must exchange all relevant information. [c1] The lead authority must also share relevant information without delay, submit a draft decision to the other authorities concerned for their opinion without delay, and take due account of their views. [c3]

Mutual assistance includes information requests and requests to carry out inspections and investigations; where appropriate, authorities must also conduct joint operations, including joint investigations and joint enforcement measures. [c2][c6]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its source: c5 for the general duty to cooperate and share information, c1 and c3 for the lead authority's duties, c2 for mutual assistance, and c6 for joint operations where appropriate.

answers.question: If a company gets my details from somewhere other than me, what else do they have to tell me, like how long they'll keep my data and where they got it?
answers.answer:
When a company obtains your personal data from somewhere other than you, it must tell you the following, subject to the exceptions below. [c1][c2][c6]

- **How long it will keep your data**, or, if that cannot be specified, the criteria used to decide that period. [c1]
- **Where your data came from**, including whether it came from publicly accessible sources, if applicable. [c1]
- Its identity and contact details, those of its representative where applicable, and its data protection officer’s contact details where applicable. [c2]
- The purposes and legal basis for processing, the categories of personal data concerned, and any recipients or categories of recipients. [c2]
- Where processing relies on Article 6(1)(f), the legitimate interests pursued by the company or a third party. [c1]
- Your rights to request access, correction, deletion or restriction of processing, to object to processing, and to data portability, plus your right to complain to a supervisory authority. [c1]
- Where processing is based on consent under Article 6(1)(a) or Article 9(2)(a), your right to withdraw consent at any time without affecting the lawfulness of processing based on consent before withdrawal. [c1]
- The existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4), and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about its logic, significance and envisaged consequences for you. [c1]
- Where applicable, intended transfers to a third country or international organisation and whether a Commission adequacy decision exists; for the transfers specified in Article 14(1)(f), it must identify the appropriate or suitable safeguards and how to obtain a copy or where they are available. [c2]

**Timing:** It must provide this information within a reasonable period after obtaining the data, no later than one month, taking account of the circumstances; if it uses the data to communicate with you, no later than the first communication, or if disclosure to another recipient is envisaged, no later than the first disclosure. [c3]

**Exceptions:** These duties do not apply where and insofar as you already have the information, or where obtaining or disclosure is expressly required by EU or Member State law that provides appropriate protection for your legitimate interests, or where legally regulated professional secrecy requires confidentiality. [c6]

An exception also applies where providing the information proves impossible or would involve disproportionate effort, or where the information obligation is likely to make the processing objectives impossible or seriously impair them; in those cases, the company must take appropriate protective measures, including making the information publicly available. [c6]
answers.reason: Each listed item, the timing rules and the exceptions match Art. 14(1), 14(2), 14(3) and 14(5) as given in the sources, and each citation is attached to a claim that its source supports.

answers.question: If a new law already required a general risk review before it was passed, does my public agency still have to do its own separate privacy risk check before starting the data handling that the law sets out?
answers.answer:
Not necessarily—but a general risk review alone is not enough to establish the exemption: a data protection impact assessment must already have been carried out as part of that review when the law was adopted. [c1]

For Article 35(1)–(7) not to apply, the processing must also be pursuant to Article 6(1)(c) or (e), have a basis in Union law or the Member State law applicable to your agency, and that law must regulate the specific processing operation or set of operations concerned. Even then, Member States may require an assessment before processing starts. [c1]

If that exemption does not apply, your agency must carry out a data protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to result in a high risk to people’s rights and freedoms, taking into account its nature, scope, context and purposes. [c3]
answers.reason: Each claim matches the cited source: c1 supports the exemption conditions and the Member State option to require an assessment, and c3 supports the high-risk DPIA duty when the exemption does not apply.

answers.question: If my information is sent to a company in another country, can I ask what protections are in place to keep it safe?
answers.answer:
Yes—if your personal data are transferred to a third country or an international organisation, you have the right to be informed of the appropriate safeguards relating to that transfer. [c1]

In the absence of an adequacy decision, a controller or processor may transfer the data only if it provides appropriate safeguards and enforceable rights and effective legal remedies are available to you. [c2][c4] Those safeguards may include binding corporate rules or standard data protection clauses. [c4]
answers.reason: Each claim matches the sources: [c1] gives the right to be informed of safeguards, [c2] and [c4] support the conditions for transfers without an adequacy decision, and [c4] lists binding corporate rules and standard data protection clauses as possible safeguards.

answers.question: Can I file a complaint about how my personal data was handled using an online form, or do I have to send a letter?
answers.answer:
Yes—if you consider that the processing of your personal data infringes the GDPR, you have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. [c3]

You do not have to send a letter: supervisory authorities must facilitate complaints through measures such as a complaint form that can be completed electronically, without excluding other means of communication. [c1]
answers.reason: Both claims are supported: Art. 77(1) [c3] gives the right to lodge a complaint, and Art. 57(2) [c1] requires authorities to facilitate complaints with an electronically completable form without excluding other means, which supports the claim that a letter is not required.

answers.question: Can a company charge me money or turn me down if I keep asking to see the personal data they hold about me?
answers.answer:
Yes, but repeated requests do not automatically justify a fee or refusal: the company must demonstrate that your requests are **manifestly unfounded or excessive**, particularly because they are repetitive. [c1] In those circumstances, it may charge a reasonable fee taking account of the administrative costs of responding, or refuse to act on the request. [c1]

Access requests are otherwise free of charge, although the company may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs for any further copies of your personal data you request. [c1][c2] You should be able to exercise your right of access easily and at reasonable intervals. [c3]

If the company refuses to act, it must tell you why without delay and at the latest within one month of receiving your request, and tell you about the possibility of complaining to a supervisory authority and seeking a judicial remedy. [c4]
answers.reason: Each claim matches the sources: Art. 12(5) for free requests, the burden of proof, and the fee or refusal options; Art. 15(3) for fees on further copies; Recital 63 for reasonable intervals; Art. 12(4) for the duty to give reasons within one month and to mention complaint and judicial remedies.

answers.question: If my complaint about a company is turned down, which data protection office tells me the outcome and does the company also get told?
answers.answer: If your complaint is dismissed or rejected, the data protection authority where you lodged it must adopt the decision, notify you, and inform the company as controller. [c1]
answers.reason: Art. 60(8) (c1) states that the supervisory authority with which the complaint was lodged adopts the decision on a dismissed or rejected complaint, notifies the complainant, and informs the controller, which is exactly what the answer says.

answers.question: Can my small business choose to appoint someone to handle data privacy compliance even if the rules don't strictly force us to?
answers.answer:
Yes. Where appointment is not required under Article 37(1), a controller or processor may voluntarily designate a data protection officer, unless Union or Member State law requires one. [c1]

The officer can be a staff member or work under a service contract, and must be selected for their professional qualities, particularly expert knowledge of data protection law and practices and ability to perform the role’s tasks. [c3][c4] Those tasks include advising on data protection obligations and monitoring compliance. [c5]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its source: Art. 37(4) allows voluntary designation (and makes it mandatory where Union or Member State law requires it), Art. 37(6) covers staff or service contract, Art. 37(5) covers professional qualities and expert knowledge, and Art. 39(1) covers advising and monitoring compliance.

answers.question: If a company I run is being investigated over a data problem, can the main privacy regulator ask regulators in other EU countries for help or team up with them to check on a business based in another country?
answers.answer:
Yes. The lead supervisory authority can ask other supervisory authorities concerned for mutual assistance at any time and can conduct joint operations, particularly to investigate or monitor the implementation of a measure concerning a controller or processor established in another Member State. [c1]

Mutual assistance includes information requests and requests for inspections and investigations, while joint operations can include joint investigations and joint enforcement measures involving regulators’ members or staff from other Member States. [c2][c3]
answers.reason: Each claim matches the sources: [c1] supports the lead authority's power to request mutual assistance and conduct joint operations, [c2] supports mutual assistance covering information requests, inspections and investigations, and [c3] supports joint investigations and enforcement measures involving staff from other Member States.

answers.question: If a company lets a computer make an important decision about me automatically, what can I ask for to make sure a real person looks at it and I can argue against the result?
answers.answer:
If the decision is based solely on automated processing and has legal effects on you or similarly significantly affects you, you generally have the right not to be subject to it. [c2] Exceptions apply where the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract, is authorised by applicable EU or Member State law with suitable safeguards, or is based on your explicit consent. [c3]

Where the company relies on contractual necessity or your explicit consent, you can ask for **human intervention by the company**, an opportunity to **express your point of view**, and a way to **contest the decision**. [c1][c3] Recital 71 also says safeguards should include an explanation of the decision and the right to challenge it. [c4]

You can also request meaningful information about the logic involved in such automated decision-making, its significance, and its expected consequences for you. [c5]

The company must tell you what action it has taken on your request without undue delay and within one month of receiving it; where necessary because of the complexity and number of requests, it may take two further months, but must notify you within the first month and explain the delay. [c6]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: c2 for the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, c3 for the exceptions, c1 with c3 for the human intervention, point-of-view and contest safeguards under points (a) and (c), c4 for the explanation, c5 for meaningful information about the logic, and c6 for the one-month deadline and two-month extension.

answers.question: Can a healthcare provider handle my sensitive health information for my treatment if the staff member involved is legally bound to keep patient details confidential?
answers.answer:
Yes, if processing your health information is necessary for your treatment, is based on Union or Member State law or a contract with a health professional, and meets the secrecy requirements below. [c1]

The information must be processed by, or under the responsibility of, a professional bound by professional secrecy, or by another person bound by secrecy, under Union or Member State law or rules established by national competent bodies. [c2] The staff member’s confidentiality obligation can therefore satisfy the secrecy requirement if it meets those conditions, but confidentiality alone is not enough: the necessity and legal-or-contractual basis must also be present. [c1][c2]
answers.reason: The answer accurately restates Art. 9(2)(h) (necessity for treatment, legal or contractual basis) and Art. 9(3) (secrecy obligation of the professional or other person), and its conclusion that secrecy alone is insufficient follows from combining the two sources, with citations matching the claims.

answers.question: If a data protection regulator in another country asks our country's regulator for help with a case, how quickly does it have to respond?
answers.answer:
Your country’s regulator must respond without undue delay and no later than one month after receiving the other regulator’s request. [c1]

It must report the results of the measures taken or, if they are still ongoing, their progress; if it refuses to comply with the request, it must give reasons. [c2]
answers.reason: Art. 61(2) in [c1] supports the 'without undue delay and no later than one month' deadline, and Art. 61(5) in [c2] supports reporting results or progress and giving reasons for any refusal.

answers.question: If a data protection regulator in one country isn't doing enough to stop a problem that urgently threatens people's privacy, can another country's regulator ask the European-level board to step in quickly?
answers.answer:
Yes. Any supervisory authority may ask the Board for an urgent opinion or an urgent binding decision if the competent supervisory authority has not taken an appropriate measure and urgent action is needed to protect people’s rights and freedoms; it must give reasons for the request, including why action is urgent. [c1]

The Board must adopt that urgent opinion or binding decision within two weeks, by a simple majority of its members. [c2]
answers.reason: Art. 66(3) [c1] supports the first paragraph (any SA may request an urgent opinion or binding decision when the competent SA has not taken an appropriate measure, with reasons including urgency), and Art. 66(4) [c2] supports the two-week deadline and simple majority adoption.

answers.question: As a small business that handles customer data, what must I do to show I'm following the privacy rules, and do I need to keep revisiting those steps as things change?
answers.answer:
As the controller, you must put appropriate technical and organisational measures in place both to comply with the GDPR and to demonstrate that compliance; those measures must reflect the nature, scope, context and purposes of your processing, and the likelihood and severity of risks to people’s rights and freedoms. [c1]

Where proportionate to your processing activities, those measures must include appropriate data protection policies. [c5] Measures could include minimising personal data processing, pseudonymising data as soon as possible, and making data processing transparent. [c4]

Yes—you must review and update your measures where necessary. [c1] Where necessary, you must also review whether processing follows the data protection impact assessment, at least when the risk represented by the processing operations changes. [c6]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: Art. 24(1) for the measures and review duty, Art. 24(2) for proportionate policies, Recital 78 for example measures, and Art. 35(11) for the DPIA review when risk changes.

answers.question: Where can I find a public list of approved data protection certifications and seals, and the standards a certifying organization has to meet?
answers.answer:
The Board must maintain a register of all data protection certification mechanisms, seals and marks and make it publicly available by appropriate means. [c2] Supervisory authorities must also publish the certification criteria and accreditation requirements in an easily accessible form. [c1] The sources do not provide a website address for either. [c1][c2]

Certification bodies must be accredited by the competent supervisory authority, the national accreditation body, or both; accreditation by the national body must follow EN-ISO/IEC 17065/2012 and additional requirements set by the competent supervisory authority. [c5]

To be accredited, a certification body must demonstrate independence and relevant expertise, commit to the approved certification criteria, establish procedures for issuing, periodically reviewing and withdrawing certifications, seals and marks, provide transparent complaint-handling procedures and structures, and demonstrate that its tasks and duties do not create a conflict of interests. [c3] Accreditation is based on criteria approved by the competent supervisory authority or the Board. [c4]
answers.reason: Each claim matches its cited source: the Board register (c2), the supervisory authority publishing criteria and requirements (c1), accreditation routes (c5), accreditation conditions (c3), and the approval of criteria (c4). The note that no website address is given is accurate.
